A diversified portfolio can cushion the blow during a correction or bear market because gains in some holdings can offset losses in others. Active investors should also avoid over-diversifying. passages.text: The stock market is a network of exchanges, such as the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, where investors buy and sell shares of publicly traded companies. Investing can seem daunting at first, but three concepts cover most of what beginners will need to know: - How the market works. - Why long-term investing tends to beat short-term trading - Why diversification matters. This guide covers each concept. How the stock market works The stock market works like a swap meet, auction house, and shopping mall rolled into one. Each comparison captures one aspect of how it functions. As a swap meet or flea market Like a swap meet, the stock market is a place where many independent participants trade directly with one another. They include individual investors and institutional investors (e.g., hedge funds, pension plans, and investment banks). Most trading takes place on major exchanges (e.g., NYSE and Nasdaq), while smaller companies often trade over the counter (OTC). As an auction house Unlike a retail store, the stock market has no fixed prices. Diversifying your portfolio Diversification means spreading your money across many investments so that no single stock or sector can sink your portfolio. In practice, that means owning a mix of stocks across different market sectors. A diversified portfolio lowers an investor’s risk and overall volatility, though it can’t eliminate the chance of loss. The trade-off is that its returns tend to be lower than what you’d earn by picking a single big winner. There are two main ways to build one, depending on whether you want to be an active or passive investor. - Active investors research stocks and assemble a collection of companies across various industries. The Motley Fool Investment Philosophy is to buy and hold at least 50 stocks. - Passive investors let a fund do the work by buying a mutual fund, index fund, or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds a diverse group of stocks. An S&P 500 index fund, for example, holds about 500 of them.

While the stock market generally moves higher over time, it doesn't do so in a straight line. Investors use these terms to describe big stock price swings: Stock market correction A decline of 10% to 20% from a recent high in a major index, like the S&P 500. Bear market A decline of 20% or more from a recent high. Bull market A rise of 20% or more from a recent low. Bull markets often last for years, driven by economic expansion. Stock market crash A sudden, steep drop in major indexes over a few days or even a single session. There’s no formal threshold. Stock market volatility How sharply prices swing up and down, often tracked with the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX). Over time, stock prices rise as companies grow their earnings along with the economy. The S&P 500 index, which tracks 500 of the largest publicly traded U.S. companies, has historically delivered average annual returns of about 10%, though individual years vary widely and include declines. Buyers state the highest price they’ll pay (the bid), sellers state the lowest they’ll accept (the ask), and a trade happens when the two meet. As a result, stock prices change constantly. Internal factors, such as a company’s earnings and growth prospects, move prices. So do external factors, such as an upcoming election or investors’ views on the economy’s direction. As a shopping mall Like a mall, the stock market is a one-stop shop. It houses all publicly listed companies, allowing investors to buy and sell any publicly traded stock. Exchanges also serve two roles. In the primary market, companies raise cash to expand by selling new shares through initial public offerings (IPOs) or later share sales, much like a retail store selling new merchandise. In the secondary market, investors resell existing shares to one another, much like a resale shop, which gives them liquidity, meaning the ability to sell when they choose. Corrections are common but often brief. According to data from Bloomberg, the average time to recovery from a 10%-20% correction is about eight months. Long-term investing vs. stock trading Some stocks deliver big gains in short periods, but they’re outliers, not the norm. Beginners are better off avoiding stock trading, especially day trading, and focusing on long-term buy-and-hold investing. Aim to hold a company’s stock for at least five years, and ideally much longer. Long-term investing beats trading for several reasons: Higher probability of positive returns The S&P 500 has risen in about 73% of calendar years since 1928, but the odds improve the longer you hold. No rolling 20-year period over the past century has produced a negative total return. Trading, by contrast, can lock in permanent losses if you buy at a peak and sell in a panic. Great companies often keep delivering strong returns long after an early gain, so cashing out after a 10% or even 100% gain can mean giving up much larger returns later. That doesn’t mean you should never sell. Here’s when to sell stocks. Benefiting from compound interest Stocks can correct and crash, but they’ve trended higher over time, and returns build on earlier returns. For example, investing $250 a month in an S&P 500 index fund that earns the historical average of about 10% a year would grow to roughly $1 million in about 36 years. Saving on taxes Stock sales are taxable unless they’re made in a tax-advantaged retirement account, such as an individual retirement account (IRA). For stocks held more than a year, the 2026 long-term capital gains rate is 0%, 15%, or 20%, depending on your income. Short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income, at rates from 10% to 37%. Frequent trading, especially in higher tax brackets, can take a big bite out of your gains.
